title: The Last Mile From a Prompt
description: Ten tools judged on the finished artifact: typeset PDFs, scheduled videos, exported archives, designed assets, screen recordings and local desktop actions.

images.alt: A desk with a finished document, a tablet and a cup of coffee
images.caption: These tools are judged on the finished artifact, not on the quality of the generated draft.

content:
# The Last Mile From a Prompt

A generated draft is not a finished job. Somewhere between a model's output and something you can send, publish, file or ship, there is a review step, an export step, a format step and often an approval step. The ten tools in this group are built around that last mile. They are not chat interfaces with a better model behind them. They are products that take a prompt, a file or a link and return a typeset page, a scheduled video, a ZIP archive, a designed asset, a recorded walkthrough or a tidy Desktop. What they share is a bias toward review and a definite end state.

## Reviewing on the finished page

[[link:/tools/2336|Papilot]] is an agentic LaTeX editor that inverts the usual workflow. You mark up the compiled PDF, selecting a sentence or boxing an equation or figure and writing what should change, and the coding agent you chose edits the LaTeX source. Each change comes back as a typeset before-and-after for you to accept, reject or comment on, one at a time. The agent receives the exact source lines without anyone needing to know which file they are in. It supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Grok, Antigravity, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen and OpenCode, is free and open source under MIT, and offers downloads for macOS on Apple Silicon and Intel plus Linux AppImage and deb packages. It is version 0.9.0 and assumes you already have a coding agent installed. The design argument is a good one: a paper is written to be read, so changes should be reviewed where they will be read.

[[link:/tools/2343|Screenplay]] handles a similar last mile for video. You ask your agent for a walkthrough, it explores the site or app and writes a short scenario, and Screenplay plays that scenario in a browser or desktop app, films it and edits it with a smooth cursor, automatic zooms, click effects, callouts, spotlight, captions, title cards and an optional voice-over. It contains no AI and needs no model key; your agent does the thinking and Screenplay does the filming and editing. A check command plays the steps quickly without filming, and a render command re-edits the last take for style, zoom, text or voice without shooting again. It requires Node 20 or newer and a one-time Chromium download, and its init command adds an MCP server and installs a guide into the agents it finds.

[[link:/tools/2344|Mago Studio]] is a local-first AI video editor for people who need more than a recording. It offers Mago Director for script-to-video work with a cast, shot list and storyboards that keep scenes consistent, and Mago Transform for frame-accurate restyling of specific frame ranges with masks, relighting and character replacement. Projects and videos stay on your machine, and renders run on your own GPU through a bundled or existing ComfyUI, with Mago Cloud models available when you sign in. A cloud render uploads only what that render needs. It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux and the app works without a GPU, though local rendering on Windows needs a capable NVIDIA card with 8 GB of VRAM and about 63 GB of free disk. The project says its code is written to be changed by AI agents.

## From one input to a set of finished assets

[[link:/tools/2337|Postraid]] turns a website or App Store link into AI UGC videos, creator reaction hooks, product demos, Instagram carousels, TikTok slideshows and memes, then schedules what you approve to TikTok, Instagram and YouTube on autopilot. The platform reads the product page once and writes each asset from a different angle, format and energy, so the examples on the site all came from the same link. It is aimed squarely at founders, creators and growth marketers. Pricing is not published in the copied landing-page text, and the output is oriented toward social ads rather than long-form video.

[[link:/tools/2342|Rivermark]] is an AI design canvas for creatives that keeps you in control, built around a brand kit with named colours and typefaces that constrain every variant. A single design produces Instagram posts, stories and wide social formats together, with layers, text, font, size, weight, alignment, colour, padding, fill and radius all editable in a properties panel. Its voice-led session lets someone think out loud while the canvas makes a headline bolder, lays out three type styles, applies the one you point at and scales the artwork. A Design API is offered for teams building products or agents. Pricing is not published in the copied landing-page text, and the workflow is built around one canvas rather than a full asset pipeline.

[[link:/tools/2341|host0]] addresses the moment after an agent has built something. It turns an HTML artifact, website, Markdown file, PDF or image into a shareable link with no repo, build pipeline or YAML. You add a skill to your agent, describe the tool you want, then say deploy and the app is live on its own URL, private until you share it and open to anyone with the link when you choose. An optional MCP connector manages, shares and locks down apps but does not deploy them. There is a free plan and a published Pro price, and the setup prompt works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Bot and other agents.

## Exports, archives and everyday actions

[[link:/tools/2338|MeetCrate]] is a Chrome and Edge extension for people with large archives of AI meeting notes. It bulk exports Read AI and Fathom meetings, transcripts, summaries and action items, as Markdown, TXT, SRT or JSON in one ZIP, with an index CSV and one file per meeting. Markdown uses YAML front matter for Obsidian and Notion, subtitles carry speaker names, and the raw API JSON is kept so nothing is lost. You can export only what is new since the last run, and an interrupted export resumes where it stopped while staying within each service's rate limits. Everything is local: files are created on your computer, nothing goes to a company server, there is no account and no trackers, and the extension uses Read AI's read-only sign-in or your own Fathom API key. It is free for 25 exported meetings in total.

[[link:/tools/2339|Nico]] is a voice-to-action personal agent for Mac. You hold right Command and say what you want, and she reads your screen, handles the file you drop on her, answers email, turns a PDF into a spreadsheet or tidies the Desktop. Replies go out only after you have seen them, files can be put back with an undo, and she works in her own browser on your Mac or in your Chrome through an extension so sites see your usual network and existing login. A watch mode checks folders, pages and your calendar and only speaks up when something is new. It runs on the ChatGPT or Claude subscription you already have with no cloud computer, and everything happens on your Mac.

[[link:/tools/2340|Cinnamon]] is a personal agent a household can share, planning, booking, watching and reminding for up to five people, with shared and private spaces that never mix. It drafts a morning inbox digest, runs appointments and renewals with reminders that arrive early, and waits on a price until you should know. Its memory policy is explicit: no hidden profile from chats, every learned fact written in plain English and reviewable, editable or deletable in one tap, scoped to the space it belongs to, and every external action stopping for approval. There are no ads and data is never used to train models. New accounts get 25 free credits, enough for roughly 15 to 25 tasks, with no credit card required.

[[link:/tools/2345|WhatYouSay]] finishes a smaller but very real job. It is a small self-hosted Node.js server that links to a WhatsApp account as a linked device, transcribes voice notes with Whisper, cleans up the text, optionally translates and summarises, and posts the result as a reply right under the note without keeping the transcripts. Transcript and summary text are never written to the database; each processed note leaves one metadata row, senders are pseudonymised after 90 days, and credentials are encrypted at rest. Users choose which notes are transcribed and can exclude contacts or groups, and a live web dashboard shows transcripts while it is open. The README carries a plain warning: it connects through Baileys, an unofficial WhatsApp Web client that can put a number at risk, and audio and text go to Groq for processing.

## The artifact is the interface

Across all ten, the model is not the product boundary. The boundary is a PDF you accept or reject, a ZIP you can unzip into your notes app, a video you can schedule, a page you can share, or a Desktop you can put back with one sentence. That is why approval shows up so often: when the output is a real action in a real account, someone has to see it first. It is also why several of these are local-first or open source, keeping files and credentials on the user's machine.

The tradeoffs are consistent too. Several are early versions with narrow platform support, a few require an existing subscription or an installed agent, and the ones that act on your behalf ask before they submit. But this is a healthier shape than an endless chat window. A tool that finishes a job can be judged on whether the job got done, and that is a standard an ordinary person can apply without knowing anything about the model behind it.
tldr: Papilot, Postraid, MeetCrate, Nico, Cinnamon, host0, Rivermark, Screenplay, Mago Studio and WhatYouSay all finish a job rather than produce a draft.
